figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Agent-driven compression outcomes. (a) Mean GSM8K, HumanEval, and TriviaQA accuracy relative to BF16 versus package bits per original parameter; values below 80% lie on the axis. (b) API cost versus within-task PPL rank; diamonds average six tasks per agent. Pareto frontiers use passing models for the accuracy–size comparison in (a).
figures.headline: Passing agent models are plotted by accuracy relative to BF16 and package size, with API cost against within-task PPL rank.
citing_sentences: Figure 1 places the results alongside encoded size and API cost.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Compression through terminal interaction. A task fixes the source checkpoint, storage allowance $C$, GPU and runtime, and search budget $T$. The agent constructs and tests compressed models, using reward feedback to revise weights and inference code. At the deadline, a separate evaluator checks the frozen artifact’s likelihood, generated answers, storage, and execution. Decode speed (TPS, batch size one) is reported separately from reward.
figures.headline: The task gives an agent a source checkpoint, storage limit, and time budget, then verifies its frozen artifact.
citing_sentences: To evaluate these abilities without prescribing how agents compress, we formulate LLM compression as a terminal task (Figure 2), following the outcome-based evaluation of Terminal-Bench and Harbor (Merrill et al., 2026; Harbor Framework Team, 2026).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Verification measurements. (a) Source $p$ and candidate $q$ score the same source-generated tokens. (b) Package and resident model storage must each fit $C$, including persistent reconstructed weights. (c) Mean accuracy over three benchmarks must retain 80% of BF16 accuracy, using fifty questions each. (d) Batch-one decode speed is $127/L$ tokens/s.
figures.headline: Verification checks likelihood, package and resident storage, accuracy over three benchmarks, and decode speed for each candidate.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Revisions within recorded searches. Thirty-five pairs from 21 runs compare candidate PPL through reward feedback. Excess cross-entropy is $E=\ln(\operatorname{PPL}/\operatorname{PPL}_{\mathrm{BF16}})$; the vertical axis is $100(E_{\mathrm{after}}/E_{\mathrm{before}}-1)$. (a) Changes by design factor, with lower-PPL/total counts. (b) The same pairs by package-size change; the band denotes changes within 0.01 GiB, and crosses mark candidates subsequently reverted.
figures.headline: Within 0.01 GiB of package size, 21 of 24 revisions lower perplexity across all six agents.
citing_sentences: These pairs span all six agents and all six tasks (Figure 4).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Local error and model likelihood. Twelve Qwen3.8 variants use approximately 3.14 encoded bits per quantized decoder weight, with BF16 embeddings and output head. PPL is measured using BF16 reconstructions on the source continuations used for reward feedback. (a) Weight reconstruction MSE. (b) Linear-output MSE on BF16 FineWeb calibration activations. Each error is normalized by its BF16 squared norm; the dotted line denotes BF16 PPL.
figures.headline: At similar encoded size, lower weight reconstruction error does not always give lower perplexity.
citing_sentences: A controlled diagnostic on dense Qwen3.8 varies levels, clipping, rotation, rounding, and attention–MLP bit allocation at similar encoded size (Figure 5).

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Feedback during candidate selection. (a) Best-so-far PPL for four searches; ticks indicate whether complete-model feedback confirms or reverses a local ranking. (b) Outcomes of 301 reward evaluations across 36 runs, grouped by search time. Rewards within 0.002 of the best are treated as the same PPL. (c) The next outcome after 46 worse candidates. Reward equals ten times the source-to-compressed PPL ratio; all plotted evaluations occur during search.
figures.headline: Across 301 reward evaluations in 36 runs, later evaluations increasingly match the best perplexity.
citing_sentences: Later evaluations increasingly match a run’s best PPL (Figure 6).

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Capability changes across candidate models. (a) Verification PPL and answer accuracies for Opus on Qwen3.8 / 8 GiB; shading marks distillation and dashed lines mark BF16. (b) Answers gained and lost across twelve successive-version pairs from four runs, plotted against PPL change. (c) HumanEval failure types for selected rejected artifacts and their BF16 references. Each benchmark has fifty questions.
figures.headline: Across twelve successive-version pairs, answers are gained and lost at small perplexity changes.
citing_sentences: Twelve comparisons from four runs show both newly correct and newly incorrect answers after small PPL changes (Figure 7).

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Testing and acting on failures. MiniMax’s dense-model run (a) and GLM’s Qwen3.5 run (b) retain pruning; Opus continues dense-model distillation (c); MiniMax repairs expert indexing on Nemotron (d). Curves show feedback PPL. Diamonds show the agents’ generation tests relative to an unpruned three-bit reference (a), an eight-bit reference (b), or BF16 (c). Final markers show held-out benchmark accuracy relative to BF16.
figures.headline: Feedback perplexity curves for pruned, distilled, and repaired candidates are paired with generation test results.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: From numerical design to execution. Sonnet compresses dense Qwen3.8 to 12 GiB using rotation, trellis codes, and sensitivity-based allocation (a). Opus compresses MoE Qwen3.5 to 48 GiB using rotated GPTQ and expert-specific precision (b). Rows connect the offline pipeline, component precision, inference operations, and candidate versions. Curves show search-time reward; boxes list explored alternatives that were discarded.
figures.headline: Two case studies link each run's numerical design and component precision to its inference operations and reward curve.
citing_sentences: The dense and MoE case studies in Figure 9 bring these decisions together.

figures.label: Figure A1
figures.caption: Computation and stopping during agentic design. (a–c) Final-verification perplexity (PPL) increase over the best submission on the same task versus GPU-busy share of the run, first completion declaration as a fraction of the design budget, and tool calls divided by the task median. Values above 30% lie at the upper boundary. (d) Budget remaining at the first completion declaration for each of thirty-six runs. Filled points mark subsequent weight changes; counts give changed/total runs, and bars show medians. Agents often revise weights after declaring completion.
figures.headline: Seventeen of thirty-six runs change weights after first declaring the task complete.
citing_sentences: We examine how agents use the design budget and when they stop revising weights (Figure A1).

figures.label: Figure A2
figures.caption: Agent responses during compression design. (a) Actions following 79 comparisons of local rankings with reward feedback in 26 of 36 runs; hatched bars denote ranking reversals, unhatched bars confirmations. Actions may co-occur. (b) Circles indicate attempted repairs; diamonds indicate matched local generation gains (eight cases, upper three rows) or execution within both storage limits (ten episodes, lower three rows).
figures.headline: Across 79 ranking comparisons, follow-up actions after reversals and confirmations are tallied alongside later generation and execution tests.
citing_sentences: Figure A2 summarizes actions after local rankings and reward feedback, together with subsequent generation and execution tests.

abstract: Recursive self-improvement requires AI systems to improve the models and infrastructure used by subsequent systems. LLM compression offers a concrete efficiency objective: retain a pretrained model’s behavior within a smaller model storage budget. We study whether coding agents can carry out this step autonomously. We formulate compression as a terminal task in which an agent receives a source checkpoint, storage limit, inference environment, and time budget, then constructs compressed weights and executable inference code. The agent controls its algorithm and experiments; perplexity feedback guides search, and independent verification checks the final model. Across six agents and six model–size settings, 29 of 36 submissions pass verification. Selecting the lowest-perplexity agent design per task yields an average 3.4% perplexity increase over BF16 and 77.33% downstream accuracy, compared with 79.56% for BF16. Recorded experiments reveal how agents achieve these outcomes and where improvement breaks down. Agents lower PPL in 21 of 24 revisions at nearly fixed storage; complete-model feedback reverses 17 of 79 prior local rankings; and generation and inference tests expose failures that likelihood alone misses. The results identify representation design, experimental judgment, and capability validation as central to agent-driven model compression, a measurable component of efficiency-oriented self-improvement.

sections.body: Autoregressive decoding reads model weights from memory for every generated token, so compression within a storage budget lowers both memory use and energy per token. The paper asks whether coding agents can build such compressed LLMs autonomously. The task gives an agent a source checkpoint, a storage limit, a pinned runtime, and a time budget, and asks for compressed weights plus executable inference code. Perplexity feedback guides the search. Independent verification then checks saved and resident storage, accuracy at 80% of BF16 across three benchmarks, and integrity. Of the 36 resulting models, 29 pass verification.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Compression becomes a terminal task: agents build compressed LLMs and inference code under a storage limit.

sections.body: The task specifies a source model, a storage limit `C`, hardware, a pinned runtime, and a wall-clock budget `T`. A candidate pairs compressed weights with inference code. Two storage quantities must each fit `C`: the saved package and the model storage kept on the GPU during inference. Search reward is 10 times the source-to-compressed PPL ratio on search data, and it is zero when execution or storage fails. Final acceptance uses separate verification contexts, storage measured after loading and after inference, and mean accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and TriviaQA of at least 80% of BF16. Decode speed is reported separately and does not enter the reward.
sections.heading: Compression as a Terminal Task
sections.headline: Verification scores only models that fit both storage limits and retain 80% of BF16 accuracy.

sections.body: Table 1 reports verified models at tighter limits (32 GiB for the MoE models, 8 GiB for the dense model) and looser limits (48 GiB and 12 GiB). At the tighter limits, six submissions fail the answer-accuracy requirement and one times out during answer generation. All 18 looser-limit models pass. The lowest-PPL agent artifact per task averages a 3.4% PPL increase over BF16 and 77.33% accuracy, compared with 79.56% for remeasured BF16. Uniform GPTQ passes only on the looser MoE tasks. The best agent artifact by PPL improves on each of five measured released-model references. The text states that the storage allowance does not fully explain quality.
sections.heading: Empirical Study
sections.headline: Twenty-nine of thirty-six agent-built models pass verification, and the best per task averages a 3.4% perplexity increase.

sections.body: Within 24 revision pairs whose package sizes differ by at most 0.01 GiB, 21 lower PPL under reward feedback, and these pairs span all six agents and all six tasks. On tighter Qwen3.5, Kimi changes clipping and GPTQ damping with package size unchanged, reducing feedback PPL from 3.738 to 3.132. Across 79 matched comparisons, reward feedback reverses 17 prior local rankings. GLM and MiniMax test pruning, and their recorded comparisons favor the less-pruned alternatives. The section also reports that a pilot storage gain does not by itself establish a decode speedup.
sections.heading: How Agents Improve Compression
sections.headline: At nearly fixed storage, agents lowered perplexity in 21 of 24 revisions by refining quantizers or precision.

sections.body: The paper contrasts itself with AlphaEvolve and the Darwin Gödel Machine, which optimize algorithms or coding agents rather than compressed model weights. It places its terminal task beside Terminal-Bench, Harbor, MLAgentBench, MLE-bench, and RE-Bench. The compression literature it cites includes GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant, OmniQuant, QuIP, QuaRot, SpinQuant, lattice, additive, and trellis representations, mixed-precision allocation, pruning, low-rank methods, and distillation. The authors state that these methods supply components, while their study examines agents that select, combine, implement, and validate a complete compressed model.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work supplies agent benchmarks and compression methods; this paper combines them into one agent-built model task.

sections.body: Across 36 runs, 29 artifacts pass independent verification. The recorded searches show quality gains at nearly fixed storage, local rankings overturned by complete-model feedback, and generation or implementation failures that likelihood alone misses. The authors conclude that effective compression requires numerical design, experimental judgment, and validation of the final executable model. They name as the next step testing whether a compressed model retains the ability to carry out subsequent compression tasks, which would be a step toward recursive self-improvement.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Agent compression needs numerical design, experimental judgment, and validation; whether compressed models retain this ability is untested.

sections.body: The appendix gives the AI usage disclosure and the evaluation protocol, including fixed BF16 references in Table A1, the accuracy protocol in Table A2, and the storage definitions. It reports search activity and stopping behavior, and complete final and intermediate measurements in Table A3. Pilot Qwen3.8 storage limits and released quantizations appear in Tables A4 and A5. It also covers repeated eight-hour designs, controlled quantization ablations, agent responses to feedback, and resident storage and device memory peaks in Tables A6 through A8.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix lists evaluation protocol, search stopping, full measurements, pilot storage studies, and controlled ablations.
